To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Obesity is a risk factor for breast carcinoma, especially postmenopausal breast carcinoma, and that the risk increases with the degree of obesity.
“Obesity and insulin resistance increase the risk of breast cancer and are associated with worse prognosis, and weight loss and exercise improve prognosis.”
the prognosis of breast cancer is worse in obese women, and that the prognosis of obese women with breast carcinoma can be improved with diet and exercise.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of diet and exercise in reducing the risk of breast cancer.
the role of estrogen in the pathogenesis of breast carcinoma and with the role of obesity in increasing the levels of estrogen and insulin.
determining whether weight reduction and increased physical activity will improve the prognosis of breast cancer patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are not yet strong enough to warrant a specific dietary regimen to reduce estrogen levels or a specific exercise program to reduce body weight or insulin resistance.
a diet and exercise program that reduces body weight, especially abdominal fat, and improves insulin resistance may reduce the risk of recurrence and mortality from breast carcinoma.
the evidence is strong enough to warrant a clinical trial of a weight reduction diet in breast carcinoma patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a diet that reduces weight by 5% and increases exercise by 20% can reduce breast cancer risk by 50% or more.
a low‐fat, low‐calorie diet and moderate exercise are beneficial for the prognosis of breast cancer patients.
the most effective way for women to lower their risk of breast cancer is to maintain a normal body weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most important dietary factors are the amount and type of fat consumed.

a diet that reduces estrogen and insulin levels, and increases the level of circulating SHBG, is a diet that is low in total and saturated fat, low in carbohydrates, and high in fiber and monounsaturated fat.
a low glycemic index diet (low GI) is associated with lower levels of circulating estrogen, insulin and insulin‐like growth factor‐1 (IGF‐1) in postmenopausal, overweight and obese women.
